name: Vinča culture
info: The Vinča culture was a Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, 5400–4500 BC, known for some of the largest settlements of prehistoric Europe, dark-burnished pottery, figurines, the Vinča symbols and the earliest known copper smelting.

facts.homeland: Southeastern Europe, mainly modern Serbia but also parts of southern Hungary, western and central Romania (Oltenia, Transylvania), western Bulgaria, eastern Croatia, eastern Bosnia, northern Montenegro and North Macedonia; key sites Vinča-Belo Brdo near Belgrade, Pločnik, Rudna Glava, Divostin, Crkvine-Stubline, Gomolava, Selevac, Tărtăria and Vršac
facts.period: 5400/5300–4500 BC on 600 radiocarbon dates (2016); phases A–D after the type site, with the “Vinča C shock” or Gradac phase (Vinča B2–C1) and a late Vinča D phase, c. 4850–4500 cal BC
facts.known: large tell settlements such as Vinča-Belo Brdo; dark-burnished, Black-topped and Rainbow Ware pottery; zoomorphic and anthropomorphic figurines; the Vinča symbols; the earliest known copper smelting and copper tools at Pločnik; copper mining at Rudna Glava; common wheat, oats and flax brought to temperate Europe
facts.sources: Excavation of the type site Vinča-Belo Brdo, discovered by Miloje Vasić in 1908; radiocarbon dating (76 dates in 1996, 155 in 2009, 600 in 2016); the syntheses of John Chapman, Colin Renfrew, Ruth Tringham, V. Gordon Childe and Milutin Garašanin; archaeogenetic studies of 2017 and 2018

t: Vinča settlements were larger than those of almost every other European culture of their time; Vinča-Belo Brdo covered 29 hectares with up to 2,500 people.
The Vinča site of Pločnik has produced the earliest copper tools in the world, though copper was used mostly for ornaments while working tools stayed of stone, bone and antler.
Whether the culture grew out of the local Starčevo culture or came with a new movement of people from Anatolia is still undecided.
dyk: The Vinča symbols incised on objects of the culture are conjectured by some to be the earliest form of proto-writing.
ev: The Vinča culture began, according to 600 radiocarbon dates published in 2016
The Divostin site was occupied twice, with an estimated 1,028 houses built
Crkvine-Stubline was founded, perhaps housing up to 4,000 people
In the Vinča D phase the centre of the network shifted from Vinča-Belo Brdo to Vršac
The Vinča network lost its cohesion and fell into decline
Miloje Vasić discovered the type site, Vinča-Belo Brdo

sections.origins:
The Vinča culture, also called the Turdaș or Vinča-Turdaș culture, is a Neolithic culture of Southeast Europe dated to 5400–4500 BC. It is named for its type site, Vinča-Belo Brdo, a large tell settlement near Belgrade discovered by the Serbian archaeologist Miloje Vasić in 1908. Radiocarbon dating has narrowed its span: 155 dates published in 2009 placed the type site at 5400/5300–4650/4600 BC, and 600 dates in 2016 placed the culture between 5400/5300 and 4500 BC.

Its origins are still debated, and Marko Porčić wrote in 2016 that there is not enough evidence to accept or reject any of the hypotheses. One, proposed by Colin Renfrew and Ruth Tringham, has it develop locally from the Starčevo culture; but the earliest southern sites seem as early as the northern ones and lack local continuity. The other, proposed by V. Gordon Childe and Milutin Garašanin, sees a second movement of people from Anatolia into the Balkans. Archaeogenetic studies of 15 individuals found mostly Y-DNA haplogroup G2a and about 90–97% Early European Farmer ancestry, closest to Neolithic Anatolia.
sections.society:
Farming brought to the region by the First Temperate Neolithic was developed further under the Vinča culture, fuelling a population boom. Settlements fell into sizes of about 1–1.9, 4–4.9 and 20–29 hectares, and some outgrew the Aegean and Near Eastern cities of a millennium later. Vinča-Belo Brdo covered 29 hectares with up to 2,500 people, Crkvine-Stubline may have held 4,000, and Parța perhaps 1,575. Early densities were 50–200 people per hectare. Yet there is no evidence of proto-urbanism or of specialised military, religious or administrative centres, though settlements had defences, and the network was probably not politically unified.

Most people worked at producing food in a mixed economy of farming, herding, hunting and foraging. Vinča farmers introduced common wheat, oats and flax to temperate Europe and made more use of barley, and there is indirect evidence for the cattle-drawn plough. Cattle mattered more than sheep and goats and were kept for milk, leather and draught. Herders took livestock to the uplands each season. Deer, boar and aurochs were hunted and carp and catfish caught. Crafts were made in the household, with little sign of specialists.
sections.beliefs:
Like other cultures of its age, the Vinča culture is distinguished chiefly by its settlement pattern and its ritual behaviour. Figurines in various zoomorphic and anthropomorphic styles were among its hallmarks, and the cohesion of its scattered settlements was kept up by the long-distance exchange of ritual items, the figurines among them. The Vinča C phase, also called the “Vinča C shock” or Gradac phase, saw an increase in ritual figurines alongside changes in pottery, settlement and metalworking; the change was strongest in the South-Moravian and Kosovian variants of the culture.

The Vinča symbols, marks incised on objects, are among the culture’s most discussed features. Some conjecture that they are the earliest form of proto-writing, a reading that remains a matter of debate. Marija Gimbutas placed the culture within her “Old Europe”, which she described as relatively homogeneous, peaceful and matrifocal. That view was widely held until the 1990s, when evidence of violent massacres and defensively enclosed settlements in the Neolithic began to emerge.
sections.arts:
The culture was particularly noted for its distinctive dark-burnished pottery. Some Vinča wares were made with considerable technical skill: a two-stage method produced pottery with a polished, multicoloured finish known as Black-topped and Rainbow Ware, and powdered cinnabar and limonite were sometimes applied to the fired clay as decoration. The figurines were made in many styles, animal and human.

Figurines also show how people dressed, in open-necked tunics and decorated skirts. Cloth was woven from flax and wool, flax becoming more important later, and buttons were made of shell or stone. In metalworking the Vinča culture featured the earliest known example of copper smelting, though it is not usually counted as Chalcolithic. Copper ores were mined on a large scale at Rudna Glava, but only a fraction was smelted and cast, into ornaments and trinkets rather than tools, which stayed of chipped stone, bone and antler. Most mined ore was probably used as powder, for pottery or for decorating the body. In the late Vinča D phase the first toggling harpoon appeared.
sections.exchange:
The Vinča region had already been settled by farming societies of the First Temperate Neolithic, such as the Starčevo culture, and the culture showed strong links with its neighbours: Karanovo in Bulgaria, Precucuteni-Tripolye A in Moldavia and Ukraine, Dimini in Greece, and the late Starčevo and early Sopot cultures in eastern Croatia. Its settlements, spread across the central Balkans, kept a high degree of cultural uniformity through the long-distance exchange of ritual items, though they were probably not politically unified.

Exchange shifted in the late Vinča D phase. The centre of the network moved from Vinča-Belo Brdo to Vršac, and the long-distance trade in obsidian from modern-day Hungary and Spondylus shell from the Aegean became more important than the exchange of figurines. Settlements, though they show no specialised military centres, had defensive works. Seasonal movement into the uplands was driven partly by the search for stone and minerals, and where these were rich, permanent upland settlements were founded that relied more on herding.
sections.legacy:
Eventually the Vinča network lost its cohesion and fell into decline. After two millennia of intensive farming, economic stress from falling soil fertility was probably partly responsible. Gimbutas argued that the decline was followed by an invasion of horse-riding Proto-Indo-European tribes from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, a view since criticised as “New Age sentiment” and prevalent until the 1990s, when evidence of Neolithic massacres and fortified settlements emerged; the debate over the culture’s end, like its origins, remains open.

The culture is remembered for some of the largest settlements of prehistoric Europe, surpassed in its time only by the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture, and for the beginnings of copper metallurgy. Its genetic profile links it to the Neolithic movement of farmers from Anatolia through the Balkans into central Europe, and a 2021 study found that Neolithic farmers, the Vinča among them, produced lower levels of inflammatory cytokines than earlier hunter-gatherers, a trait that has passed into the immune system of modern Europeans. Its type site, Vinča-Belo Brdo, is today a suburb of Belgrade.

summary: The Vinča culture flourished in the central Balkans from about 5400 to 4500 BC, its farmers building some of the largest settlements of prehistoric Europe. Known for dark-burnished pottery, figurines, the debated Vinča symbols and the earliest known copper smelting, its network declined after two millennia of intensive farming.
